name: Tara Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Haddad and Sons Home Supply, a family-owned distributor of furniture and homewares. We serve about 120 independent shops across the region. I'm in early, and I go through the container arrivals, check what's come in against what we ordered, and ring the factories when it doesn't match. In the afternoon I see reps, and on Thursdays I walk the warehouse with the foreman, because I trust my eyes more than a printout.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that this is a family firm and that I've been part of it for twenty-six years. I like choosing a sofa line that I know will sell in a small town. What wears me out is competition from the online giants, which sell cheaper than we can buy, and the pressure to do more with fewer people. And Mr. Haddad's son, who wants to change everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because the loudest voices were wrong again. At work I'd say let's get back to selling well and buying carefully. At the mosque committee I'd say we should stick to what we know and look after one another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it doesn't fix the real problem, which is cheap online furniture. Haddad's sales have dropped for three years running. My boss Mr. Haddad has kept me on through three bad years, and I'd never leave him, but loyalty doesn't pay the electricity bill. I'm 58, on less than buyers at the big chains, and there's almost nowhere else locally to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the way I do. I'd cut the supplier list to the ones I trust and push those for better terms. At home, Yusuf and I would stay frugal, with no new car and no holidays, and I'd keep a small envelope of cash in the house for emergencies. I'd also keep going to the community kitchen on Fridays, because that's how I stay steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, with a heavy feeling. It's not AI that bothers me. It's the quiet way a shop closes and nobody says anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the owner's son wanting changes. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger son, Karim, wants a website and an app and an AI system. His father says yes to keep the peace. I say we're buying and selling furniture, not building a robot. But I'm careful with Karim, because he'll be my boss soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the household's money look like if something goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two weeks' worth, in the bank. Yusuf is a shift manager at a hardware shop, and that wage is steady. But the mortgage is still big and our daughters have their own bills. We don't take anything from the government, and I'd rather not.

say: I'd say good: the loudest voices were **wrong again**.
At the community committee I'd say **look after one another**.
think: Cheap online furniture is the **real problem**; sales have dropped three years running.
Loyalty to Mr. Haddad is deep, but it **doesn't pay** the electricity bill.
do: Cut my supplier list to the ones I **trust** and push them on terms.
Stay **frugal** and keep an emergency cash envelope.
Keep serving at the community **kitchen** on Fridays.
feel: **Heavy but okay**; I fear a quiet shop closure more than any robot.
S0.quote: My boss Mr. Haddad has kept me on through three bad years, and I'd never leave him, but loyalty doesn't pay the electricity bill.
fieldNote: Her loyalty is to a **family firm**, and her worry is the firm's survival, not technology.
Has an old-fashioned financial reflex: cash envelope, no handouts, frugality.

steps.text: Cut the supplier list to trusted factories and push for better terms
Stay frugal with no holidays and keep an emergency cash envelope
Lean on the community kitchen and family for small help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been through machines before and we're still here. I'd tell the family firm that a person's word still counts. At the mosque I'd say we should keep teaching the young to work and be useful, whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I learned this trade by walking factory floors and shaking hands. I won't learn it again by typing into a box. I think the screen takes the ordering and the forecasting, and Karim will use it to justify a smaller team. I'm the most senior buyer, which means the most expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying the old way and keep my best suppliers close. I'd refuse the AI training unless Mr. Haddad told me directly it was needed. I'd also pick a second route: a small stall selling quality homewares at the Saturday market, just something Yusuf and I could run. It might bring in 400 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Defensive, I'd say. Like someone is walking through my house and rearranging things. I'd be polite and furious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be cut first at home if your pay dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cancelling the extras. We'd stop the small gift to our daughter Layla and her baby each month, which would break my heart. We'd cut the phone plan, change the washing machine repair into a swap with a neighbour. And I'd stop buying anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hamid, in the warehouse, who is 61 and not far off retirement. He can't read the screens well. I'd sit with him, and I'd try to arrange for him to keep a role that's about people and carrying, not clicking. But I can't promise it.

say: I'd say we've been through machines before and **a person's word** still counts.
At the mosque I'd say we must keep teaching the young to **work**.
think: I won't learn the trade again by **typing into a box**.
Karim will use the screen to justify a **smaller team**, and I'm the dearest buyer.
do: Keep buying the **old way** and keep my best suppliers close.
Refuse the AI training unless **Mr. Haddad** says it's needed.
Start a Saturday **market stall** for quality homewares, maybe 400 a month.
feel: **Defensive**, as if someone is rearranging my house; polite and furious.
S1.quote: I learned this trade by walking factory floors and shaking hands. I won't learn it again by typing into a box.
fieldNote: A **proud refusal**: her skills are relationships and her answer is to defend them, not retool.
The market stall is a traditional, work-over-handouts side plan, small but real.

steps.text: Keep buying the old way and refuse AI training unless told directly
Start a Saturday market stall selling quality homewares
Stop the monthly gift to Layla and cancel the phone plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone's good and that nobody asked for it. At work I'd say people matter more than machines. In public I'd say there should be a pause, though I don't think anyone would listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd lose the job, and the firm would shrink to a few people and a computer. Karim would call it modern, and his father would be too tired to argue. The warehouse would survive three more years than the office, but I'm in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years isn't enough for my family or my firm to work out who feeds whom. We'd go back to what we always did, which is lean on each other. Yusuf and I would pool with our daughters and live as cheaply as we could. I'd ask Mr. Haddad if there's any role for me in the warehouse, and I'd take a lower wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, truly. I'd pray a lot, and I'd try not to show it. I'd feel like a leaf on a river.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughters, Layla and Maryam, that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd gather them all at my table and say: we'll stay together. I'd tell them, don't be ashamed to ask for help, but don't expect it from outsiders. I'd say we will work with our hands if we need to. I'd make a big pot of food, because that's what we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who made it and the people who pushed it, the big tech firms and the investors. Not Mr. Haddad. And not the government, which has more problems than it can fix. But I'd blame myself a little for not seeing it coming.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for anyone's good and nobody asked for it.
In public I'd call for a **pause**, though nobody would listen.
think: I'd lose the job, and the firm would shrink to **a few people** and a computer.
The warehouse outlasts the office by about **three years**, but I'm in the office.
do: Pool money with our **daughters** and live as cheaply as we can.
Ask Mr. Haddad for a **warehouse role**, even at a lower wage.
Lean on the **community**, and cook for the whole family.
feel: **Frightened**, like a leaf on a river; I'd pray a lot.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough for my family or my firm to work out who feeds whom. We'd go back to what we always did, which is lean on each other.
fieldNote: Her instinct is **family and community**, not government or retraining; she'd work with her hands.
Blames the makers and investors, never her employer, a strong sign of loyalty.

steps.text: Pool money with our daughters and lean on the community
Ask Mr. Haddad for a lower-paid warehouse role
Live as cheaply as we can on Yusuf's wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is some mercy, and we should use it well. I'd say at work that we should look after our people and our customers first. I'd probably go back to the mosque committee and see what we can do about training the young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to see my granddaughter start school, and I'd want to still have a job when she does. I'd be 63, which is still too young to stop with the money we have. I think I could be pushed out in year three or four, and I'd have to find some work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every penny I could, 200 a month, which means doing without. I'd check what the state pension would be at 63 and plan from there. I'd also ask Mr. Haddad, honestly, whether he sees a place for me. And I'd take a short course in book-keeping, because small shops always need someone honest to keep their books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A steady sort of worry. Not panic. I'd feel there's time, and that makes it a long wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why book-keeping, and not learning the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I wouldn't be learning to type into a box, I'd be learning a trade that's old and honest. A small shop will always need a person to look at the numbers and tell the truth. It doesn't need an app. And Yusuf could help with it, he's good with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger people in the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn something with their hands, and something about money. Don't depend on a company to look after you. Work hard and keep a small reserve. And stay close to your family.

say: I'd say five years is **some mercy**, and we should use it well.
I'd go back to the committee about **training the young**.
think: Five years lets me see my **granddaughter** start school, if I still have a job.
I could be **pushed out** in year three or four.
do: Save **200 a month** by doing without.
Ask Mr. Haddad honestly if there's a **place for me**.
Take a short **book-keeping** course for small shops.
feel: **A steady worry**, not panic; the time makes it a long wait.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to see my granddaughter start school, and I'd want to still have a job when she does.
fieldNote: Chooses a **quiet, honest trade**, book-keeping, over the tools she distrusts; the logic is her values.
More time gives her space to plan, but not enough to relax: she still expects to be pushed out.

steps.text: Save 200 a month by doing without
Take a short book-keeping course for small shops
Ask Mr. Haddad if there's a place for me in the plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we've got time, but time is only worth something if we use it. I'd tell the family firm to put money away. At the mosque I'd say let's teach our young to work with their hands and with their heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I have ten years, I'll spend them working and putting money by, because I won't take handouts and I won't ask my daughters either. I'd be 68. I think I'd leave at 65, and the firm may not even last that long if online keeps eating our sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and cut the debt first, then save 250 a month toward a small cushion. I'd take on the book-keeping side of Haddad's as a part of my role, so the firm needs me for more than buying. I'd help Layla get her own savings going. And I'd keep Yusuf at his work as long as his back lets him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier than the others. There's a long road ahead and I can walk it. I wouldn't call it calm, but it's bearable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the firm worry you more than the technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years of savings still isn't a lot, and the firm is the bigger risk than the machine. If Haddad's closes, I don't need AGI to lose my job. Those are the things that keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you advise your daughters about money and work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep a tight budget and a small reserve, don't buy what you can't pay for. And find a trade that needs a person present, like care or repair. A thing that's hands and trust is slower to be copied.

say: I'd say good, we've got time, but it's only worth something if we **use it**.
I'd tell the family firm to **put money away**.
think: I'll spend the ten years working and putting money by, with **no handouts**.
The firm may not last to 65 if online keeps **eating our sales**.
do: Clear debt first, then save **250 a month**.
Take on Haddad's **book-keeping** so the firm needs me for more than buying.
feel: **Steadier** than the others; not calm, but bearable.
S4.quote: If I have ten years, I'll spend them working and putting money by, because I won't take handouts and I won't ask my daughters either.
fieldNote: The firm's survival, not AI, is her main threat; **ten years** doesn't remove the thin cushion.
Pride in self-reliance runs through every answer: no handouts, no asking her children.

steps.text: Clear debt first, then save 250 a month
Take on Haddad's book-keeping as part of my role
Help Layla start her own savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits before my family or my firm can do anything. What would help is a firm that lasts, a few months in the bank, and a way for people to work, not wait for handouts. Apprenticeships and jobs in small shops, that's what I'd like.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't hate the machines. I hate being told my forty years don't count. I know people, I know factories, and I know what sells in a small town. Somebody should ask me what I know before they decide what to replace.

headlineQuote: I don't hate the machines. I hate being told my forty years don't count.
portrait: Tara Usman, 58, is the **senior buyer** at a family-owned furniture and homewares distributor serving 120 shops.
She's loyal to the owner, never uses AI, and has **under a month saved** with a mortgage still running.
She's traditional and free-market, wants **work and apprenticeships** over handouts, and trusts family and community.
Her mood stays anxious in most worlds and becomes **alarmed** when AGI arrives in two or five years.
She'd refuse the tools, take on **book-keeping** and market-stall work, and pool money with her family.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because it hits before her firm or family can adapt.
whatWouldHelp: A **firm that lasts**, a few months in the bank, and real jobs and apprenticeships, not handouts.
